sites.name: St. Thekla of Blachernai
sites.summary: A modest Blachernai church, later a mosque, now barely traceable
sites.description: A small church in the Blachernai quarter, later turned into a mosque and now barely traceable, traditionally identified with the Toklu Dede Mescidi.

sites.name: Palace of the Porphyrogennetos
sites.summary: The city's best-preserved Byzantine palace, standing tall against the land walls
sites.description: The best-preserved Byzantine palace in the city, a tall three-story block wedged into the land walls and built in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century. Recently restored inside.

sites.name: Monastery of Manuel the Armenian
sites.address: Derviş Ali, Arı Sk. No:2, 34087 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A little-known monastery tied to a ninth-century general, later the Kefeli Mosque
sites.description: A monastery traditionally linked to the ninth-century general Manuel the Armenian, generally identified with the building later known as the Kefeli Mosque.

sites.name: Theotokos Pammakaristos
sites.summary: A Komnenian church whose mosaic-filled side chapel rivals Chora
sites.description: A Komnenian monastery church best known for its side chapel, whose fourteenth-century mosaics are among the finest in the city. It was the seat of the Patriarchate for over a century after 1453.

sites.name: Holy Savior in Chora
alternateNames: Church of the Holy Saviour in Chora
sites.address: Dervişali, Kariye Cami Sk. No:6, 34087 Fatih/İstanbul
sites.summary: Home to the finest late-Byzantine mosaics and frescoes anywhere in the city
sites.description: A monastery church tucked up by the land walls, rebuilt in the Komnenian period and famous for the dazzling fourteenth-century mosaics and frescoes paid for by Theodore Metochites. If you see only one thing for Byzantine art in the city, make it this.

sites.name: Palace of the Kantakouzenoi
sites.address: Near the land walls, Fatih, İstanbul
sites.summary: Fragmentary remains of a Palaiologan aristocratic palace by the walls
sites.description: A Palaiologan palace associated with the powerful Kantakouzenos family, surviving only in fragments near the land walls.

sites.name: St. Theodosia
sites.summary: A tall middle-Byzantine church above the Golden Horn, now the Gül Mosque
sites.description: A tall middle-Byzantine church on the slope above the Golden Horn, traditionally identified with St Theodosia and now the Gül Mosque. Get an excellent view of the building from the Golden Horn ferry boat.

sites.name: St. John the Forerunner in Trullo
sites.summary: A modest late-Byzantine church by the Pammakaristos, now a mosque
sites.description: A small late-Byzantine church near the Pammakaristos, now the Hirami Ahmet Paşa Mosque.

sites.name: Church of St. George - Ecumenical Patriarchate
sites.address: Dr. Sadık Ahmet Cd., Fener, Fatih, İstanbul
sites.summary: The living seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, home to precious Byzantine relics
sites.description: The patriarchal church of St George in the Fener, seat of the Ecumenical Patriarch since the early seventeenth century. The building itself is post-Byzantine, but it holds important Byzantine relics and furnishings.

sites.name: Christ Pantepoptes
sites.summary: The best-preserved Komnenian church in the city, founded by Alexios I's mother
sites.description: A late-eleventh-century monastery church founded by Anna Dalassene, mother of Alexios I, and the best-preserved Komnenian church in the city. Now the Eski İmaret Mosque.

sites.name: Christ Pantokrator
sites.address: Zeyrek, İbadethane Sk. No:2, 34083 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: The great Komnenian imperial monastery and mausoleum, now the Zeyrek Mosque
sites.description: A vast twelfth-century monastery of three linked churches, founded by John II Komnenos and his empress Eirene as a dynastic burial place and hospital. Now the Zeyrek Mosque and a UNESCO site.

sites.name: St. Theodoros
sites.address: Hoca Gıyasettin, Vefa Caddesi Tirendaz Sokak, 34134 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A middle-Byzantine church in Vefa with a fine Palaiologan porch, now a mosque
sites.description: A middle-Byzantine church in Vefa, its handsome outer narthex added in the Palaiologan period and still keeping fragments of mosaic. Now the Vefa Kilise Mosque.

sites.name: Monastery of Constantine Lips
sites.address: Akşemsettin, Adnan Menderes Vatan Blv., 34091 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A tenth-century church later doubled into a Palaiologan imperial mausoleum
sites.description: A monastery of two joined churches: the north church founded by the admiral Constantine Lips in 907, the south added by the early Palaiologoi as a dynastic mausoleum. Now the Fenari İsa Mosque.

sites.name: St. Polyeuktos
sites.address: İskender Paşa, Kavalalı Sk., 34080 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: Ruins of Anicia Juliana's showpiece church, out-built only by Hagia Sophia
sites.description: The excavated ruins of a huge and lavish early-sixth-century church built by the aristocrat Anicia Juliana, briefly the grandest church in the city until Hagia Sophia eclipsed it. Its carved fragments were carried off as far as Venice. Fenced off, but largely unguarded, the ruins are mostly used by neighbors as a trash can and toilet.

sites.name: Holy Apostles
sites.summary: The vanished imperial mausoleum-church, model for St. Mark's in Venice
sites.description: Once the second church of the city and the burial place of the emperors, a great cruciform five-domed church that inspired St. Mark's in Venice. It was pulled down after 1453 for the Fatih Mosque, so nothing survives above ground. Truly intrepid searchers may find more success in the courtyard of the Istanbul Archaeology Museum, which contains monumental porphyry sarcophagi, almost certainly Imperial resting places, almost certainly taken from Holy Apostles.

sites.name: Galata Tower
sites.address: Bereketzade, Galata Kulesi Sk., Beyoğlu, İstanbul
sites.summary: The famous Galata hilltop tower, a Genoese rebuild of a Byzantine original
sites.description: The landmark tower crowning the Galata hill. The present tower is a Genoese rebuild of 1348, replacing an earlier Byzantine tower that anchored the Galata defenses.

sites.name: Galata Walls
sites.summary: Scattered remains of the walls that once ringed Genoese Galata
sites.description: The fortifications that once ringed the Genoese colony of Galata across the Golden Horn. Only scattered fragments and a few towers survive among the streets.

sites.name: St. Benoit
sites.address: Kemankeş Karamustafa Paşa, Karaköy, Beyoğlu, İstanbul
sites.summary: An old Latin church of Genoese Galata, still in use
sites.description: A Latin (Catholic) church in Galata founded in the early fifteenth century, one of the oldest continuously used churches in the city, though its roots are Genoese rather than Byzantine.

sites.name: Kastellion Substructures
sites.address: Kemankeş Karamustafa Paşa, Kemankeş Cd. No:23, 34425 Beyoğlu/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: Vaults of the fortress that held the Golden Horn chain, now under a mosque
sites.description: The vaulted substructures of the Byzantine castle that anchored the great chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn, now beneath the Yeraltı (Underground) Mosque in Karaköy.

sites.name: Church of Ss. Dominic and Paul
sites.summary: A Genoese Gothic Dominican church in Galata, now the Arap Mosque
sites.description: A large Dominican church built in the early fourteenth century in Genoese Galata, later converted into the Arap Mosque. Gothic rather than Byzantine, but a key monument of Latin Constantinople.

sites.name: Palazzo di Venezia
sites.summary: The Venetian bailo's palace in Pera, echoing Venice's grip on the late city
sites.description: The historic residence of the Venetian bailo in Pera, today part of the Italian consulate: a reminder of Venice's dominant role in late Byzantine Constantinople.

sites.name: The Milion
sites.address: Alemdar, Divanyolu Cd. No:2, 34110 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: The stub of the arch from which all roads in the empire were measured
sites.description: The surviving fragment of the Milion, the domed archway from which all distances in the empire were measured.

sites.name: Hagia Eirene
sites.address: Cankurtaran, Topkapı Sarayı No:1, 34122 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: An early church, never converted to a mosque, keeping its stark iconoclast interior
sites.description: One of the oldest churches in the city, rebuilt by Justinian after the Nika riots and again in the eighth century. It never became a mosque, so its bare interior and iconoclast cross-apse survive intact, inside the Topkapı grounds.

sites.name: Hodegetria Monastery and Ayazma
sites.summary: Home of the Hodegetria, Constantinople's holiest icon, and its sacred spring
sites.description: The monastery that housed the Hodegetria, the city's most venerated icon of the Virgin, together with its holy spring. It stood near the sea walls below the acropolis; only the spring is really traceable today.

sites.name: Column of Leo
sites.summary: A vanished fifth-century honorific column of the emperor Leo I, whose fragments may be seen in Topkapi Palace
sites.description: A now-lost honorific column raised for the emperor Leo I in the fifth century, one of the many imperial columns that once punctuated the city's squares. Fragments may be seen in the second courtyard of Topkapi Palace.

sites.name: Column of the Goths
sites.summary: A Roman victory column still standing in Gülhane, commemorating a victory over the Goths
sites.description: A tall Roman victory column standing in Gülhane Park, raised to mark a triumph over the Goths in the late third or early fourth century. One of the oldest monuments still standing in the city.

sites.name: Column of Marcian
sites.summary: A standing fifth-century column of the emperor Marcian, the "Maiden's Stone"
sites.description: A standing fifth-century honorific column raised for the emperor Marcian, tucked into a side street in Fatih and known locally as the Kıztaşı.

sites.name: Hagia Sophia
sites.address: Sultan Ahmet, Ayasofya Meydanı No:1, 34122 Fatih/İstanbul
sites.summary: Justinian's world-changing domed cathedral, the masterpiece of Byzantine architecture
sites.description: Justinian's great domed church, finished in 537 and for nearly a thousand years the largest edifice in the world. The scale of the interior still stops people in their tracks. Notable mosaics from over the Byzantine centuries remain, including a striking Deesis. Unfortunately it has regressed into a mosque from the museum it was. Ensure you plan your visit around blocked times.

sites.name: The Hippodrome and Sphendone
sites.address: Küçük Ayasofya, Nakilbent Sk. 29a, 34122 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: The city's chariot-racing arena and political cockpit; its curved end still stands
sites.description: The great chariot-racing arena and social heart of the city, laid out by Septimius Severus and completed by Constantine. Its curved southern end, the Sphendone, still stands in massive substructure, and three monuments of its central barrier survive.

sites.name: Great Palace Peristyle
sites.address: Sultanahmet Mahallesi Kabasakal Cad. Arasta Çarşısı Sok. No. 53, Sultan Ahmet, Torun Sk. No:21, 34122 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: The Great Palace's dazzling sixth-century mosaic courtyard, now a museum
sites.description: The mosaic-paved peristyle courtyard of the Great Palace, its floor crowded with vivid scenes of hunting, games and daily life. Now sheltered in the Great Palace Mosaic Museum.

sites.name: Bukeoleon Palace
sites.summary: The Great Palace's marble sea-facade, still standing in the shore walls
sites.description: The sea-front wing of the Great Palace on the Marmara shore, its marble balcony windows still hanging in a stretch of the sea walls. It took its name from a harbor marked by a bull-and-lion sculpture.

sites.name: Ss. Sergius and Bacchus
sites.summary: Justinian's experimental "Little Hagia Sophia," now a mosque
sites.description: An inventive domed church built by Justinian early in his reign, long called "Little Hagia Sophia" for its resemblance to the great church. Now the Küçük Ayasofya Mosque, but note the carved Greek writing in the stonework.

sites.name: Column of Constantine
sites.summary: Constantine's porphyry column, still standing where he founded his new capital
sites.description: The round forum that Constantine laid out when he refounded the city was marked at its center by his great porphyry column: still standing, fire-scarred and iron-hooped, as the Çemberlitaş. While the forum itself is gone, the courtyard of the Istanbul Archaeology Museum contains a colossal Gorgoneion (Medusa head) carved on a massive marble archivolt, which was the keystone of a monumental forum arch. These gorgons' twins may be found in the Basilica Cistern, reused as column bases.

sites.name: Forum of Theodosius
sites.summary: The city's grandest forum, its carved column drums still strewn round Beyazıt
sites.description: The largest of the city's forums, laid out by Theodosius I on the model of Trajan's Forum in Rome. Carved fragments of its columns lie scattered around Beyazıt Square.

sites.name: Arch of Theodosius
sites.summary: Ruined triumphal arch of the Forum of Theodosius, its knobbly columns still visible
sites.description: The monumental arch that spanned the Forum of Theodosius, its distinctive column drums carved with peacock-eye motifs, now displayed where they fell beside Beyazıt Square.

sites.name: Aqueduct of Valens
sites.summary: The city's landmark Roman aqueduct, still striding across the main boulevard
sites.description: The great double-tiered aqueduct that strides across the valley between two of the city's hills, completed under Valens in the 370s and kept in use for well over a thousand years. It still leaps over the main boulevard.

sites.name: Kontoskalion and Eleutherios Harbors
sites.summary: The Marmara harbors whose Yenikapı dig unearthed a fleet of sunken ships
sites.description: The city's great southern harbors on the Marmara, silted up and built over long ago. Excavations at Yenikapı for the metro spectacularly uncovered the Theodosian harbor with dozens of sunken ships.

sites.name: The Myrelaion
sites.address: Mesih Paşa, Ordu Cd. Beyazıt, 34130 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A tidy tenth-century palace church that ended up as an emperor's mausoleum
sites.description: A compact tenth-century church built by the emperor Romanos I Lekapenos next to his palace, later serving as his family mausoleum. It sits on top of a huge earlier rotunda, which you can still see underneath.

sites.name: Theotokos Kyriotissa
sites.address: Kalenderhane, 16 Mart Şehitleri Cd. No:11, 34134 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A Komnenian church layered over older ones, now the Kalenderhane Mosque
sites.description: A Komnenian domed church raised over a jumble of earlier structures near the aqueduct of Valens, and the place where fragments of a rare fresco cycle of St. Francis came to light. Now the Kalenderhane Mosque.

sites.name: St. Andrew of Crete in Krisei
sites.address: Sümbül Efendi, Koca Mustafapaşa Cd. No:169, 34107 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A much-altered late-Byzantine convent church, now the Koca Mustafa Paşa Mosque
sites.description: An old monastery church dedicated to St. Andrew of Crete, remodelled in the Palaiologan period and heavily altered when it became the Koca Mustafa Paşa Mosque.

sites.name: Gastria Monastery
sites.address: Koca Mustafapaşa, Teberdar Sk. No:11, 34098 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: Fragments of a small monastery tied to St Helena, now a tiny mosque
sites.description: The scanty remains of the small monastery of the Gastria, traditionally linked to St. Helena, surviving as the little Sancaktar Mosque.

sites.name: Hospital Church Ese Kapi
sites.summary: A ruined late-Byzantine hospital-church by the walls
sites.description: A ruined late-Byzantine church near the land walls, thought to have belonged to a monastery with a hospital, later the Ese Kapı Mosque.

sites.name: The Golden Gate
sites.summary: The land walls' triumphal marble gateway, now inside the Yedikule fortress
sites.description: The great ceremonial gate in the land walls through which triumphant emperors entered the city, a triple marble arch later swallowed into the Ottoman fortress of Yedikule.

sites.name: The Marble Tower
sites.summary: The marble-clad tower where the land walls meet the sea
sites.description: The tower that marks the seaward end of the land walls where they meet the Marmara, faced in marble and once linked to a small imperial retreat.

sites.name: St. Mary of Zoodochos Pege
sites.summary: The ancient healing-spring shrine outside the walls, still drawing pilgrims
sites.description: The famous shrine of the life-giving spring outside the walls, a place of pilgrimage since Justinian's day. The present church is a nineteenth-century rebuild, but the holy spring with its sacred fish endures.

sites.name: Monastery of the Studion
sites.address: Yedikule, İmam Aşir Sk. No:1, 34107 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: The city's oldest church, heart of Byzantine monasticism, now a roofless ruin
sites.description: The city's oldest surviving church, a fifth-century basilica of St. John at the great Stoudios monastery, long the powerhouse of Byzantine monasticism. It stands roofless as the İmrahor ruin.

sites.name: Anastasian Walls
sites.summary: Anastasius's "long wall" guarding the city's approaches far out in Thrace
sites.description: The long wall thrown across Thrace some sixty-five kilometers west of the city, built under Anastasius I to screen the capital's approaches. Long stretches survive out in the countryside, although more than half the stone was reused over the centuries. Best found in the wooded areas stretching toward Evcik Beach.

sites.name: Yoros Castle
sites.summary: A Byzantine-Genoese fortress guarding the Bosphorus's Black Sea mouth
sites.description: A commanding fortress on the hill above the northern Bosphorus, held in turn by Byzantines, Genoese and Ottomans, guarding the strait's entrance from the Black Sea.

sites.name: Anadolu Hisari
sites.summary: Bayezid I's Bosphorus fortress, built to strangle Byzantine Constantinople
sites.description: A compact fortress on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, built by Bayezid I in 1394 to blockade Constantinople. It's Ottoman work, but it is part of the story of the city's fall.

sites.name: Rumeli Hisari
sites.summary: Mehmed II's 1452 fortress that sealed the city's fate before the conquest
sites.description: The great fortress Mehmed II threw up on the European shore in 1452 to cut Constantinople off from the Black Sea, the final noose before the siege of 1453.

sites.name: Leander's Tower
sites.summary: The islet tower off Üsküdar, once anchoring a Komnenian Bosphorus chain
sites.description: The little tower on its islet off Üsküdar, where Manuel I Komnenos raised a tower to anchor a chain across the Bosphorus. The present building is far later, but the site is ancient.

sites.name: Forum of Arcadius
sites.summary: Arcadius's forum, remembered by the buried base of its great spiral column
sites.description: The seventh-hill forum of Arcadius, once dominated by a tall spiral column carved like Trajan's. Only the massive column base survives, half-buried in a back street.

sites.name: Forum of the Ox
sites.summary: A vanished forum on the main avenue, named for a bronze ox
sites.description: One of the great squares strung along the main avenue of the city, the Forum of the Ox took its name from a bronze ox said to have been used as a place of execution. Nothing survives.

sites.name: Cistern of Theodosius
sites.summary: A restored fifth-century cistern of Theodosius II, now open to visitors
sites.description: A restored, open-to-visitors cistern built by Theodosius II, its brick vaults carried on rows of columns. Long hidden, now handsomely lit as the Şerefiye Cistern.

sites.name: Monastery Annex and Kasim Aga
sites.address: Derviş Ali, Koza Sk. No:8, 34087 Fatih/İstanbul, Türkiye
sites.summary: A small monastery annex by the walls, later the Kasım Ağa Mosque
sites.description: A small Byzantine building near the land walls, an annex of an unidentified monastery, later the Kasım Ağa Mosque.

sites.name: Germigny-des-Prés Oratory
sites.summary: A Carolingian oratory keeping France's only Byzantine-technique Carolingian mosaic
sites.description: A rare survivor of the Carolingian age, this little square oratory was built in 806 by Theodulf of Orléans, a scholar at Charlemagne's court. Its apse mosaic of the Ark of the Covenant, which is the only Carolingian mosaic left in France, is worked in Byzantine technique, though the building itself was heavily rebuilt in the 1860s.

sites.name: Aachen Cathedral
sites.summary: A 9th century church with mosaics, modeled on San Vitale in Ravenna
sites.description: Built in the early 9th century and later much expanded, the core of the church was the original chapel of the Palace of Charlemagne. It was consciously modeled on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, one of the finest flowerings of Byzantine art.

sites.name: Périgueux Cathedral
sites.address: Place de la Clautre, 24000 Périgueux, France
sites.summary: A five-domed French cathedral consciously copying Byzantine Venice, largely rebuilt in the 1800s
sites.description: The most Byzantine-looking church in France: a Greek cross roofed with five domes on pendentives, echoing St. Mark's in Venice and the lost Holy Apostles in Constantinople. Raised in the twelfth century, but so thoroughly rebuilt by Paul Abadie between 1852 and 1900 that most of what you touch is Second Empire masonry.

sites.name: St. John's Convent
sites.summary: A Carolingian convent keeping Switzerland's finest early murals, on Italo-Byzantine models
sites.description: A Benedictine convent in a Grisons valley on the Italian border, traditionally credited to Charlemagne and now a UNESCO site. Its church holds the greatest cycle of Carolingian figurative murals in Switzerland, painted around 800 on late-antique and early-Byzantine models carried north through Italy.

sites.name: St. Martin's
sites.summary: A village church roofed by a rare Romanesque painted ceiling in Byzantinizing style
sites.description: A plain Romanesque hall church on the old Viamala route, famous for what hangs overhead: an early-twelfth-century painted wooden ceiling of 153 panels, one of only two Romanesque painted ceilings in Europe to survive largely intact. Its frontal, linear figures follow Byzantine and Italo-Byzantine conventions carried north through Lombardy.

sites.name: Abegg-Stiftung
sites.summary: A premier textile museum holding and conserving Byzantine silks, south of Bern
sites.description: Not a Byzantine site but one of the world's foremost textile collections and research centers, in the hills south of Bern. Founded by Werner and Margaret Abegg in 1961, it preserves and studies Byzantine samite and figured silks: the fragile medium in which much Byzantine luxury art actually survives. Seasonal opening only.

sites.name: Lambach Abbey
sites.summary: A Benedictine abbey concealing Austria's oldest frescoes, in Byzantinizing style
sites.description: A Benedictine abbey founded in 1056, now mostly Baroque, but its west choir hides the oldest monumental frescoes in Austria: a later-eleventh-century cycle on the infancy of Christ, rediscovered in 1957. The weightless figures and gold grounds descend from Byzantine models absorbed in northern Italy and Salzburg. Shown only on guided tours.

sites.name: St. John's Chapel
sites.summary: A Styrian chapel with vivid Byzantinizing frescoes, including a curious cat-and-mouse war
sites.description: A small, austere Romanesque chapel above a Styrian village, holding one of Austria's best-preserved fresco cycles, painted around 1160 in a distinctly Byzantine style. Its oddest scene is a "war of cats and mice," tentatively linked to the Byzantine mock-epic Katomyomachia.

sites.name: Imperial Crown (Reichskrone)
alternateNames: Imperial Crown of the Holy Roman Empire
sites.summary: The Holy Roman emperors' crown, its enamels emulating Byzantine court goldwork
sites.description: The coronation crown of the Holy Roman emperors, an octagonal crown of eight hinged gold plates most often dated to the later tenth century. Four plates carry cloisonné enamels of Christ and the Old Testament kings, worked in the Byzantine manner. Thus, a Western imperial object whose most prestigious technique and imagery came straight from Byzantine court goldwork. The dating is disputed.

sites.name: Mikulčice-Valy
sites.summary: A Great Moravian citadel tied to the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius
sites.description: A principal stronghold of ninth-century Great Moravia on the Morava river, where excavation has uncovered a palace and the foundations of about a dozen churches, which is the densest concentration of Great Moravian church architecture known. Ensure you see the mission of Cyril and Methodius, the brothers from Thessaloniki sent by Constantinople in 863. The buildings are Moravian, not Byzantine, and survive only as foundations.

sites.name: Uherské Hradiště-Sady
sites.summary: The probable ecclesiastical heart of Methodius's Moravian church, now foundations
sites.description: "Methodius's Hill" above the Staré Město agglomeration long identified with Veligrad, the likely chief center of Great Moravia. Excavation found a cruciform church that grew by stages, and the leading candidate for the heart of Methodius's Moravian church, and perhaps his seat and burial. Foundations only; the burial claim is probable, not proven.

sites.name: Veszprémvölgy Greek Nunnery
sites.summary: A Byzantine-rite nunnery founded by St Stephen, with Hungary's only Greek royal charter
sites.description: The ruins of a Byzantine-rite nunnery in the valley below Veszprém, one of Hungary's earliest religious houses, founded about 1018 by King Stephen I for Basilian nuns. Its Greek foundation charter is the only surviving document Stephen issued in Greek, following Byzantine form. A genuine Byzantine-rite royal foundation on Hungarian soil.

sites.name: Visegrád Greek Monastery
sites.summary: A Byzantine-rite royal monastery of the "Tourkia" province, above the Danube Bend
sites.description: A Basilian (Byzantine-rite) monastery of St. Andrew above the Danube Bend, founded around the mid-eleventh century by King Andrew I, who had spent years of exile at Kyiv and married a Rus princess. It belonged to the short-lived Byzantine church province of "Tourkia" in Hungary, and survives archaeologically rather than in elevation.

sites.name: Holy Crown of Hungary
sites.address: Hungarian Parliament, Kossuth Lajos tér 1-3, 1055 Budapest, Hungary
sites.summary: A Byzantine crown from 1070s Constantinople, now the lower band of Hungary's Holy Crown
sites.description: The lower band of the Hungarian Holy Crown, called the corona graeca, is genuine Byzantine imperial goldwork made in Constantinople in the 1070s, a diplomatic gift from Emperor Michael VII Doukas to King Géza I. Its cloisonné enamels show a Byzantine court program, with Géza pointedly ranked below the emperors. One of only two surviving Byzantine crowns.

sites.name: Church of the Acheiropoietos
sites.summary: A fifth-century Thessaloniki basilica, standing near full height and UNESCO-listed
sites.description: One of the oldest churches in the city, an early-Christian basilica raised over a Roman baths complex and preserved almost to its original height. The building is datable by its bricks and mosaics to about 450–470. One of the fifteen Thessaloniki monuments on the UNESCO list, it keeps a thirteenth-century wall-painting of the Forty Martyrs in the south aisle.

sites.name: Aula Palatina
sites.summary: Constantine's vast Roman audience hall at Trier, essential pre-Byzantine context
sites.description: A colossal Roman palace basilica built around 300–310 under Constantius Chlorus and Constantine, the imperial audience hall of the tetrarchic capital and now the Protestant Church of the Redeemer. This is Constantinian late-Roman rather than Byzantine proper, given that it predates Constantinople itself, but it is essential context for the Constantinian world.

sites.name: Rotunda of St George
sites.address: Knyaz Aleksandar Dondukov Blvd 2, 1000 Sofia, Bulgaria
sites.summary: Sofia's oldest building, a Roman rotunda holding a millennium of Byzantine frescoes
sites.description: A red-brick domed rotunda on a square base, standing amid the ruins of late-Roman Serdica and the oldest building in Sofia, in baptismal use since the fourth century. Its draw is the stacked frescoes: a fourth-century Roman-Byzantine floral layer, a tenth-century Bulgarian layer with angels, an eleventh–twelfth-century frieze of prophets, and a fourteenth-century donor bishop.

sites.name: Panagia Ekatontapyliani
sites.summary: A rare standing Justinianic church on Paros, linked to a Hagia Sophia architect
sites.description: A rare standing Justinianic complex: a fourth-century basilica splendidly rebuilt with a dome under Justinian, who is said to have set Isidorus (one of Hagia Sophia's architects) over the work, carried out by his apprentice Ignatius. The sixth-century iconostasis survives, and the adjacent baptistery with its cruciform font is nearly unique in Greece. The "Hundred Doors" name carries the legend of a hidden hundredth door.

sites.name: Duomo di Salerno
sites.summary: A Norman cathedral carrying a Byzantine bronze door and apse mosaics
sites.description: Built 1080–85 under Robert Guiscard over an older church and consecrated in 1084 by Gregory VII, who died in Salerno. Two genuine Byzantine elements survive: a bronze main door cast in Byzantium and fragmentary apse mosaics attributed to Archbishop Alfanus I. Byzantine work on a Norman-Romanesque church.

sites.name: Monte Cassino
sites.summary: The Benedictine mother-abbey that imported Byzantine mosaicists, their work now lost
sites.description: The Benedictine mother-abbey, and a key node in the westward flow of Byzantine craftsmen. Abbot Desiderius summoned mosaic workers from Constantinople to decorate his new basilica (dedicated 1071) and had local artists trained by them, having earlier ordered a bronze door from Constantinople in 1066. Unfortunately, the Desiderian church is completely gone, destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt.

sites.name: Euphrasian Basilica
sites.summary: A Justinianic cathedral at Poreč with gold mosaics rivalling Ravenna's
sites.description: A peer of Ravenna: a three-naved basilica built 539–554 under Bishop Euphrasius in Justinian's reign, over the foundations of earlier churches. Its apse carries gold mosaics that are among the finest early-Byzantine mosaics in Europe. UNESCO-listed as the only fully preserved early-Christian cathedral complex of its era.

sites.name: Cathedral of Monreale
sites.address: Piazza Guglielmo II 1, 90046 Monreale PA, Italy
sites.summary: The vast Norman cathedral clad in over 6,000 square meters of Byzantine mosaic
sites.description: The climax of Norman-Byzantine Sicily, documented to 1174 under William II and raised over an earlier Greek church. It is famous for over 6,000 square meters of gold-ground Byzantine mosaics — among the largest and best-preserved cycles in Europe — their iconographic program entrusted to Byzantine models and craftsmen.

sites.name: Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio
sites.summary: Palermo's most Byzantine church, with Constantinopolitan mosaics and a living Greek rite
sites.description: The most Byzantine building in Palermo, built in 1143 for George of Antioch, Grand Admiral under Roger II, on an east-oriented cross-in-square plan. Its mosaics were made by artists brought from Constantinople working here about 1140–55, including the famous panel of Roger II crowned directly by Christ. It now belongs to the Italo-Albanian Byzantine rite.

sites.name: Royal Palace and Palatine Chapel
sites.summary: Roger II's palace chapel, a Byzantine mosaic core in a Norman building
sites.description: Roger II's palace chapel, commissioned in 1132 on an older chapel and mosaiced over the following decades. Its oldest mosaics, in the crossing, dome and three apses, are taken to be by craftsmen from Constantinople and carry Greek inscriptions. A Norman-Byzantine UNESCO listing.

sites.name: Cathedral of San Demetrio Megalomartire
sites.address: Piazza Vittorio Emanuele, 90037 Piana degli Albanesi PA, Italy
sites.summary: The living cathedral of Sicily's Italo-Albanian Byzantine-rite church
sites.description: A sixteenth-century rebuild that is now the cathedral of the Eparchy of Piana degli Albanesi, or the Italo-Albanian Church of the Byzantine rite in Sicily. Its interior mixes Western Novelli frescoes with an Eastern iconostasis and side-aisle icons. Not Byzantine-era fabric, but a genuine living Byzantine rite.

sites.name: Byzantine Walls and Towers of Tyndaris
sites.address: Tyndaris archaeological zone, 98066 Patti ME, Italy
sites.summary: Ancient promontory walls at Tyndaris, reinforced in the Byzantine era near the Black Madonna shrine
sites.description: The ancient walls of Tyndaris on the promontory were reinforced in the late-imperial and Byzantine era. Tyndaris was a Byzantine bishopric where the first Black Madonna shrine rose around the eighth century, before the Arabs destroyed the town in 835–836.

sites.name: Syracuse Cathedral
sites.summary: A Byzantine cathedral built into a standing Greek temple on Ortigia
sites.description: A genuine Byzantine church-conversion wrapped around a Greek temple: built over the fifth-century-BC Doric Temple of Athena, whose columns are still embedded in the nave walls. In the seventh century Bishop Zosimo walled up the outer columns and opened the inner chamber as a nave under Byzantine rule, reversing the orientation and adding three eastern apses. Later a mosque, then Norman.

sites.name: Basilica di Santa Sofia a Via Boccea
alternateNames: Ukrainian Catholic Basilica of Saint Sophia
sites.address: Via di Boccea 478, 00166 Roma RM, Italy
sites.summary: A 20th-century Byzantine-Revival Ukrainian basilica in Rome, echoing Hagia Sophia of Kyiv
sites.description: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic basilica of Rome, dedicated to Holy Wisdom. Begun by Cardinal Josyf Slipyj after his 1963 release from the gulag and built 1967–69 to plans echoing Hagia Sophia of Kyiv, its interior is entirely mosaiced on gold by Sviatoslav Hordynsky. A deliberate twentieth-century Byzantine Revival in the living Ukrainian rite.

sites.name: St. Cyril's Church
sites.summary: Kyiv's best-preserved Rus church after the Hagia Sophia, with 800 m² of 12th-century fresco
sites.description: After the Hagia Sophia, the only Kyiv church surviving from the Rus period in essentially its original form. Built as the Olgovichi family burial vault around the mid-twelfth century, with two-meter walls that let it double as a fortress, it keeps some 800 square meters of twelfth-century frescoes.

sites.name: Saint Michael’s Monastery Chapel
sites.summary: A 1108 Byzantine-mosaiced cathedral, dynamited in 1936 and rebuilt in 1999.
sites.description: Founded 1108–1113 and decorated by Byzantine masters whose mosaics ranked with Hagia Sophia's, reputedly the first church in Rus with a gilded dome. The Soviets dynamited the cathedral in 1936, and the present building is a 1999 reconstruction. The genuinely Byzantine material is the original mosaics stripped before demolition, some now in the Hagia Sophia, some only recently returned. Headquarters of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.

sites.name: Dormition Cathedral
sites.summary: The Caves Monastery's mother church of 1073, destroyed in 1941 and rebuilt in 2000.
sites.description: The mother church of the Caves Monastery, built 1073–1078 and the architectural model imitated across Rus, its foundation legend crediting builders and an icon sent from Constantinople by the Theotokos herself. Blown up in 1941 and rebuilt in 2000; more original fabric survives in the nearby Trinity Gate Church.

sites.name: Golden Gate
sites.summary: Yaroslav's Constantinople-modeled city gate of c.1037, rebuilt over its ruins in 1982
sites.description: The ceremonial main gate of Yaroslav the Wise's Kyiv, built around 1037 in the same campaign as Hagia Sophia and consciously echoing the Golden Gate of Constantinople, with a Church of the Annunciation set over the passage. It survived the 1240 Mongol siege only as a ruin. What stands today is a 1982 reconstruction raised over the authentic eleventh-century remnants.

sites.name: Church of the Saviour at Berestove
sites.summary: A Rus-era church by the Lavra, later repainted 'in the Greek manner' under Petro Mohyla
sites.description: This church has a core dating to the late eleventh or early twelfth century and long a burial place of the ruling house. Its Byzantine dimension is twofold: a Rus-Byzantine core, and a striking layer of seventeenth-century frescoes by Greek painters brought in under Metropolitan Petro Mohyla, whose tomb is inside.

sites.name: Chersonesus
sites.summary: Byzantium's great Black Sea city, where Volodymyr of Kyiv was baptized around 988
sites.description: A Greek colony that became the largest city on the northern Black Sea coast and seat of the theme of Cherson, refortified by Justinian as the empire's window onto the steppe. Around 988 Prince Volodymyr of Kyiv took the city and, by the dominant tradition, was baptized here before marrying the princess Anna and causing the Christianisation of Rus. Its ruins include several Byzantine basilicas. UNESCO-listed since 2013.

sites.name: Mangup
sites.address: Mangup-Kale plateau, Bakhchysarai Raion, Crimea, Ukraine
sites.summary: The mountain capital of Theodoro, the last Byzantine statelet, which fell in 1475
sites.description: A dramatic flat-topped mountain fortress fortified under Justinian to shield Cherson, known early on as Doros and later the capital of the Principality of Theodoro - a small Greek-speaking Orthodox statelet that considered itself heir to Byzantium. Theodoro outlived Constantinople itself, holding out until the Ottomans stormed it in December 1475, extinguishing the last fragment of the Byzantine political world. The plateau keeps walls, a cave monastery, cisterns, and the princes' citadel.

sites.name: Eski Kermen
sites.address: Eski-Kermen plateau, Bakhchysarai Raion, Crimea, Ukraine
sites.summary: A 6th century cave town near Mangup, with rock-cut Byzantine churches and frescoes
sites.description: A ruined cave town on a limestone plateau near Mangup, developed as a fortified settlement within the same system protecting Cherson. The site contains hundreds of rock-cut rooms, cisterns, staircases, and Byzantine churches keeping fragments of medieval fresco.

sites.name: Inkerman Cave Monastery of St. Clement
sites.summary: An 8th-century Crimean cave monastery of icon-fleeing monks, tied to St. Clement of Rome
sites.description: A cave monastery carved into the cliffs above the Chorna River, probably founded in the eighth century by icon-venerating monks fleeing Iconoclasm. Tradition ties it to St. Clement of Rome, martyred in the Crimea around AD 101, whose relics were reputedly recovered here and later carried west by Cyril and Methodius. The rock complex sat beneath the Theodorite fortress of Kalamita; the standing monastic buildings are largely nineteenth-century, the community refounded in 1991.

sites.name: Sudak Fortress
sites.summary: A Byzantine port and bishopric beneath a spectacular Genoese fortress shell
sites.description: The imposing hilltop fortress retains its Genoese form, but Sougdaia was a major Byzantine port and Orthodox metropolitan see long before Italian rule, with Byzantine inscriptions in its churches into the twelfth century. Genoa seized it in 1365 and raised the double-walled citadel that dominates the town, before the Ottomans took it in 1475.

sites.name: Aluston Fortress
sites.summary: A Justinianic coastal fortress, now fragmentary walls amid the Alushta resort
sites.description: One of the coastal strongholds Procopius says Justinian built in the sixth century, extending the imperial defensive line that anchored on Cherson and Mangup. Sections of the fortress walls and a tower still stand amid the modern resort town.

sites.name: Gorzuvity Fortress
sites.summary: Justinian's coastal fort at Gurzuf, its traces on the Genoese Rock
sites.description: A sixth-century Byzantine fortress built under Justinian alongside Aluston to hold the southern Crimean shore. Traces of the fortification occupy the Genoese Rock promontory at Gurzuf, later reused by the Genoese as they absorbed the Byzantine coast. Fragmentary remains only.

sites.name: Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi Fortress
sites.address: Akkerman Fortress, Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Odesa Oblast, Ukraine
sites.summary: The "White Castle" of Byzantine Asprokastron, surviving as a name and a buried layer
sites.description: This was the Greek colony of Tyras, later Roman and Byzantine, where in late antiquity was built a fort called Asprokastron, "White Castle," a name which linguists may note is echoed in the Slavic Bilhorod, Turkish Akkerman, and Romanian Cetatea Albă. But the great fortress on the site is thirteenth-to-fifteenth-century Genoese, Moldavian, and Ottoman; the Byzantine layer is documented and partly excavated rather than standing.

sites.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
sites.summary: A world-class Byzantine collection in New York, from goldwork to icons
sites.description: Not a Byzantine site but the holder of one of the great Byzantine collections outside Europe: gold jewelry, silver, ivories and icons, plus a reconstructed church treasure. Its medieval galleries and The Cloisters carry the story of Byzantine art to a wide public.
sites.hours: 10:00–17:00 Sun, Mon, Tue, Thu; 10:00–21:00 Fri, Sat; closed Wed

sites.name: Dumbarton Oaks Museum
alternateNames: Dumbarton Oaks Research Library and Collection
sites.summary: The leading Byzantine studies center in the Americas, with a fine coin and silver collection
sites.description: The foremost center for Byzantine studies in the Americas, this is a research institute, library and museum in Georgetown with a superb collection of Byzantine coins, seals, silver and jewelry. Its scholarship underpins much of the field.

sites.name: Exarchic Greek Monastery of Santa Maria di Grottaferrata
alternateNames: Abbey of Santa Maria di Grottaferrata
sites.address: Corso del Popolo 128, 00046 Grottaferrata RM, Italy
sites.summary: A Byzantine-rite Greek abbey near Rome, keeping the Greek liturgy unbroken since 1004
sites.description: A Greek (Byzantine-rite) monastery in the Alban Hills founded in 1004, and the last surviving Italo-Greek abbey of the many that once dotted southern Italy. It has kept the Byzantine liturgy in Greek without a break for over a thousand years, and preserves an important library and scriptorium.

sites.name: Cathedral of Agios Demetrios
sites.summary: Mystras's cathedral of St Demetrios, tied to the last Byzantine emperor
sites.description: The cathedral of Byzantine Mystras, dedicated to St. Demetrios, begun in the 1260s and later given an upper gallery and domes. Its frescoes span the city's golden age, and a marble slab in the floor marks where, by tradition, the last emperor Constantine XI was proclaimed in 1449.

sites.name: Agioi Theodoroi (Vrontochion)
sites.summary: Mystras's earliest great church, a domed octagon of the 1290s
sites.description: The oldest of the great monastic churches of Mystras, built around 1290–95 in the Vrontochion monastery, this octagon-domed church is based on the model of Hosios Loukas and Daphni.

sites.name: Hodegetria / Aphentiko (Vrontochion)
sites.summary: The Aphentiko, a hybrid domed basilica with superb early-Palaiologan fresco
sites.description: The Aphentiko, or Hodegetria church of the Vrontochion, built around 1310–22, is a bold hybrid of basilica below and domed cross above, with some of the finest early-Palaiologan frescoes in Greece.

sites.name: Peribleptos Monastery
sites.summary: A rock-built Mystras monastery with a complete, refined late-Byzantine fresco cycle
sites.description: A monastery church of the mid-fourteenth century built into the rock at the lower edge of Mystras, whose interior keeps one of the most complete and refined late-Byzantine fresco cycles anywhere.

sites.name: Pantanassa Monastery
sites.summary: Mystras's last and still-living church of 1428, a final flourish of Byzantine art
sites.description: The last church built at Mystras, consecrated in 1428 and the only monastery still inhabited, by a small community of nuns. Its elegant belfry and richly colored frescoes mark the final flowering of Byzantine art on the eve of the fall.

sites.name: Hagia Sophia
sites.summary: The palace chapel of the despots of Mystras, high in the upper town
sites.description: The palace church of the despots of Mystras, built around the mid-fourteenth century high in the upper town, serving as chapel royal and a burial place for members of the ruling house.

sites.name: Evangelistria
sites.summary: A small, finely carved funerary church of late Mystras
sites.description: A small, finely built funerary church of the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century at Mystras, notable for the quality of its carved marble.

sites.name: Palace of the Despots
sites.summary: The rare surviving palace of the despots of the Morea
sites.description: The sprawling palace of the despots of the Morea, one of very few Byzantine secular palaces to survive, built in stages from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries around an L-shaped plan with a great throne hall. Extensively restored.

sites.name: Castle of Mystras
sites.summary: The 1249 Frankish castle whose hill became Byzantine Mystras
sites.description: The Frankish castle crowning the hill of Mystras, built in 1249 by the Villehardouin prince of Achaea and soon ceded to the Byzantines, who grew the city down the slope beneath it.

sites.name: Laskaris House
sites.summary: An aristocratic mansion of old Mystras, associated with the Laskaris family
sites.description: An elegant mansion of two stories, with arches, vaults, and a balcony, historically associated with the aristocratic Laskaris family.

sites.name: Hagia Sophia
sites.summary: A cliff-edge domed church crowning Monemvasia's upper town
sites.description: The domed church crowning the upper town of Monemvasia, founded in the twelfth century on the model of Daphni and standing dramatically at the cliff edge. Later a mosque, now restored. Be careful when visiting; the cliff is not secured by fencing or other barriers.

sites.name: Elkomenos Christos
sites.summary: Monemvasia's lower-town cathedral of Christ Elkomenos
sites.description: The main church of Monemvasia's lower town, dedicated to Christ Elkomenos ("the dragged to crucifixion"), of Byzantine origin and much rebuilt, but still the town's cathedral.

sites.name: Kastro fortifications
sites.summary: The fortifications of Monemvasia's fortress-rock, layered from Byzantium onward
sites.description: The walls and gates of the great fortress-rock of Monemvasia, a Byzantine stronghold from the sixth century whose upper and lower towns were defended by successive Byzantine, Frankish, Venetian and Ottoman fortifications.

sites.name: Archaeological Collection
sites.summary: Monemvasia's small museum of Byzantine sculpture and finds, in a former mosque
sites.description: A small museum in the restored former mosque of Monemvasia's lower town, displaying Byzantine architectural sculpture, ceramics and finds from the site.

sites.name: Geraki castle and frescoed churches
sites.summary: A Frankish castle and frescoed Byzantine churches, a quiet echo of Mystras
sites.description: A Frankish hilltop castle of the 1250s with a scatter of small Byzantine and post-Byzantine churches on the slopes below, several keeping frescoes. This site can be compared to a quieter, less-visited Mystras.

sites.name: Agioi Theodoroi
sites.summary: An inner-Mani church of 1075, among the peninsula's earliest dated
sites.description: A small domed church at Vamvaka in inner Mani, dated by inscription to 1075, it ranks among the earliest firmly dated churches in the peninsula and is notable for its carved marble.

sites.name: Agios Stratigos
sites.summary: A major inner-Mani church above Boularioi, rich in 11th–12th-century fresco
sites.description: A domed church above Boularioi, one of the more important Byzantine monuments of Mani, keeping extensive frescoes of the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

sites.name: Agios Panteleimon
sites.summary: A Boularioi chapel with some of Mani's oldest, most archaic frescoes
sites.description: A small church at Boularioi preserving some of the oldest wall-paintings in Mani, in an archaic style generally dated to the tenth or early eleventh century.

sites.name: Agios Prokopios
sites.summary: A small 12th-century country chapel near Episkopi in Mani
sites.description: A small Byzantine chapel in the country near Episkopi in inner Mani, of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Episkopi (Agios Georgios)
sites.summary: A domed Mani church of St. George that served as a local bishop's seat
sites.description: The "Episkopi" of Agios Georgios in the Koita area, a domed Byzantine church that once served as a local episcopal seat, keeping frescoes.

sites.name: Agioi Sergioi and Bakchos
sites.summary: A Middle Byzantine church of Ss. Sergios and Bacchos near Koita
sites.description: A small Byzantine church near Koita dedicated to Saints Sergios and Bacchos, with wall-paintings of the Middle Byzantine period.

sites.name: Agitria
sites.summary: A remote domed church of the deep Mani, with 12th–13th-century fresco
sites.description: The Agitria, a domed Byzantine church near the tip of the deep Mani, keeping good frescoes of the twelfth to thirteenth centuries in a remote setting.

sites.name: Vlacherna
sites.summary: A 12th-century Virgin church near the Mani port of Mezapos
sites.description: A Byzantine church near the little port of Mezapos, dedicated to the Virgin of Blachernae, of the twelfth century and noted for its carved decoration and frescoes.

sites.name: Taxiarches
sites.summary: A 12th-century Archangels church at Charouda in Mani
sites.description: A small domed church of the Archangels at Charouda, of the twelfth century, with frescoes.

sites.name: Agia Varvara
sites.summary: A domed Mani church of St. Barbara, with well-preserved 12th-century fresco
sites.description: A domed church at Erimos dedicated to St. Barbara, keeping a well-preserved fresco cycle of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Agios Nikolaos
sites.summary: A small 12th-century St. Nicholas church at Briki
sites.description: A small Byzantine church of St. Nicholas at Briki, of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Agia Triada
sites.summary: A small 12th-century Holy Trinity church at Briki
sites.description: A small Byzantine church of the Holy Trinity at Briki, of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Agios Ioannis
sites.summary: A small 12th-century St. John church at Keria
sites.description: A small Byzantine church of St. John at Keria, of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Metamorphosis
sites.summary: An 11th–12th-century Transfiguration church at Kato Gardenitsa
sites.description: A church of the Transfiguration at Kato Gardenitsa, of the eleventh or twelfth century, with carved decoration.

sites.name: Agios Nikolaos
sites.summary: A 12th century church with gargoyles near the south-facing cliffs
sites.description: A 12th century church and bell tower standing on its own in mostly open country near the south-facing cliffs of Mani. Don't miss the gargoyles.

sites.name: Agies Maries
sites.summary: A small 12th-century church at Kato Gardenitsa
sites.description: A small Byzantine church at Kato Gardenitsa, of the twelfth century.

sites.name: Agios Ioannis Prodromos
sites.summary: A St. John church in Areopoli, its Byzantine core later folk-painted
sites.description: A Byzantine church of St. John the Baptist in Areopoli, the little capital of the Mani, its Byzantine core later overlaid with the folk-style painting typical of the region.

sites.name: Church of the Taxiarches
sites.summary: Areopoli's Archangels church, where the 1821 Greek revolt was proclaimed
sites.description: The church of the Taxiarches in Areopoli, of Byzantine origin, famous for the relief carvings of its façade; on its steps the Mani raised the banner of the Greek revolt in 1821.

sites.name: Agios Athanasios
sites.summary: A small Byzantine St. Athanasios church in Areopoli
sites.description: A small Byzantine church of St. Athanasios in Areopoli, later repainted in the local manner.

sites.name: Agios Nikolaos
sites.summary: A Byzantine St. Nicholas church in church-rich Proastio
sites.description: A Byzantine church of St. Nicholas at Proastio, a village unusually rich in churches, its Byzantine core overlaid with later painting.

sites.name: Agioi Theodoroi
sites.summary: A Byzantine church of the Theodores at Kambos
sites.description: A Byzantine church of the Holy Theodores at Kambos in the Messenian Mani, with frescoes.

sites.name: Agios Ioannis Prodromos
sites.summary: A Byzantine St, John church at Milia in the Messenian Mani
sites.description: A Byzantine church of St. John the Baptist at Milia in the Messenian Mani.

sites.name: Church of the Transfiguration of the Savior
sites.summary: A sophisticated 11th-century domed church in rural Messenia
sites.description: A fine eleventh-century domed church of the Constantinopolitan type, unusually sophisticated for a rural Messenian setting; earthquake-damaged but partly restored.

sites.name: Holy Church of the Virgin Zoodochos Pege Samarina
sites.summary: A well-preserved 12th-century domed church near Androusa
sites.description: The Panagia Samarina near Androusa, a well-preserved twelfth-century domed church incorporating antique spolia. One of the best Middle Byzantine churches of Messenia.

sites.name: Androusa Castle
sites.summary: A 13th-century Frankish castle of Messenia, later Byzantine and Ottoman
sites.description: A well-preserved Frankish castle of the thirteenth century in Messenia, later held by the Byzantines of the Morea and the Ottomans.

sites.name: The Church of the Dormition of Theotokos at Merbaka
sites.address: Epar.Od. Tirinthas - Neo Ireo 3, Ag. Triada 210 55, Greece
sites.summary: A 12th-century domed church at Merbaka, a key Argolid monument
sites.description: The Koimesis church at Merbaka in the Argolid, a domed cross-in-square church of the twelfth century and one of the region's principal Middle Byzantine monuments.

sites.name: Agia Moni
alternateNames: Ιερά Μονή Ζωοδόχου Πηγής Άριας - Αγία Μονή
sites.summary: A 1149 convent church near Nafplio, beside an ancient sacred spring
sites.description: The convent of Agia Moni near Nafplio, whose domed church of 1149 is a refined example of Middle Byzantine architecture; a sacred spring in the grounds is identified with the ancient Kanathos.

sites.name: Acronauplia
sites.summary: The much-layered acropolis fortress of Nafplio, Byzantine among its phases
sites.description: The rocky acropolis of Nafplio, fortified from antiquity through the Byzantine, Frankish, Venetian and Ottoman periods; the Byzantine and later walls still crown the peninsula above the town.

sites.name: Larissa Castle
sites.summary: The hilltop castle of Argos, Byzantine among its many builders
sites.description: The castle crowning the Larissa hill above Argos, built on ancient foundations and developed by Byzantines and later Franks and Venetians into a major stronghold of the Argolid.

sites.name: Church of the Assumption
sites.summary: The old cathedral of Tegea, of Byzantine origin, set in an ancient theater
sites.description: The old cathedral of Tegea, a church of Byzantine origin (much rebuilt) set within the ruins of an ancient theater, long the episcopal seat of the region.

sites.name: Acrocorinth
sites.summary: The mighty acropolis-fortress above Corinth, Byzantine among its many holders
sites.description: The towering acropolis of Corinth, one of the great fortresses of Greece, held and rebuilt by Byzantines, Franks, Venetians and Ottomans in turn above the ancient city.

sites.name: Iviron Monastery
sites.summary: The great Georgian monastery of Athos, founded around 980
sites.description: One of the senior monasteries of Athos, founded around 980 by Georgian monks (hence its name, "of the Iberians") and long the great Georgian house of the Holy Mountain. It holds the revered icon of the Panagia Portaitissa and a rich library.

sites.name: Gelati Monastery
sites.summary: David the Builder's royal Georgian monastery, with a Byzantine-style apse mosaic
sites.description: The great monastery founded in 1106 by King David the Builder near Kutaisi, a royal foundation and medieval academy whose main church keeps a superb apse mosaic of the Virgin in Byzantine style: a rare survival tying Georgian art directly to Constantinople. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Church of St. Donatus
sites.summary: Zadar's monumental 9th-century rotunda, raised on the Roman forum
sites.description: The great circular pre-Romanesque rotunda of Zadar, built in the ninth century on the old Roman forum, this is a monumental round church descended from Byzantine and Carolingian models, and the symbol of the city.

sites.name: Salona
sites.summary: The ruined early-Christian capital of Dalmatia, abandoned around 614
sites.description: The ruined capital of Roman Dalmatia and a major early-Christian center, with excavated basilicas, a baptistery and a vast cemetery of martyrs; it flourished into the Byzantine period before the Avar-Slav sack around 614.

sites.name: Diocletian's Palace and Cathedral of St. Domnius
sites.summary: Diocletian's vast palace, his mausoleum reborn as Split's cathedral
sites.description: The colossal fortified palace Diocletian built around 300, later filled by the medieval town of Split; the emperor's own mausoleum was turned into the Cathedral of St. Domnius, so a persecutor of Christians lies displaced by the saint he martyred. Late-Roman fabric with a continuous Byzantine-to-medieval afterlife.

sites.name: Cathedral of St. Tryphon
sites.summary: Kotor's 1166 cathedral of St. Tryphon, on a 9th-century predecessor
sites.description: The Romanesque cathedral of Kotor, consecrated in 1166 on the site of an earlier ninth-century church housing the relics of St. Tryphon, the city's patron.

sites.name: Church of St. Luke
sites.summary: A 1195 Kotor church shared by Catholic and Orthodox rites
sites.description: A small church of 1195 in Kotor blending Romanesque and Byzantine forms, which long served both Catholic and Orthodox congregations. An emblem of the town's mixed-rite heritage. Fragments of Byzantine-style fresco survive.

sites.name: Church of St. Mary Collegiate
sites.summary: A 1221 Kotor church on an early-Christian basilica, with Byzantine-tinged fresco
sites.description: The collegiate church of St. Mary in Kotor, built in 1221 on the foundations of an early-Christian basilica, keeping remains of Byzantine-influenced frescoes.

sites.name: Church of St. Michael
sites.summary: A small medieval Kotor church with Byzantine-style fresco fragments
sites.description: A small medieval church in Kotor raised over earlier remains, preserving fragments of Byzantine-style wall-painting.

sites.name: Voroneț Monastery
sites.summary: The "Sistine Chapel of the East," with blue-ground frescoes on a 1488 Moldavian church
sites.description: Founded by Stephen the Great in 1488 and famous for the intense "Voroneț blue" of its exterior frescoes. A vast Last Judgment across the west wall is the masterpiece of Moldavia's painted churches, whose art descends from late-Byzantine models. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Moldovița Monastery
sites.summary: A 1532 painted monastery whose walls show the Siege of Constantinople.
sites.description: A fortified Moldavian monastery of 1532 whose outer walls carry brilliant frescoes, including a famous Siege of Constantinople: a defiant memory of the fallen Byzantine capital painted in the Carpathian foothills. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Humor Monastery
sites.summary: A 1530 Moldavian church in warm red-brown exterior fresco
sites.description: A small Moldavian monastery of 1530, its exterior washed in warm reddish-brown frescoes including an Akathist to the Virgin and a Siege of Constantinople. UNESCO-listed among the painted churches.

sites.name: Sucevița Monastery
sites.summary: The largest and last painted Moldavian monastery, with a famous Ladder of Virtue
sites.description: The largest and last of the great painted monasteries, fortified like a castle and completed around 1585, its green-toned frescoes include a celebrated Ladder of Virtue. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Arbore Church
sites.summary: A 1503 boyar church with fine green-toned exterior frescoes
sites.description: A small boyar church of 1503 at Arbore, its exterior frescoes dominated by green and celebrated for their fine drawing, even among the painted churches of northern Moldavia. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Probota Monastery
sites.summary: A 1530 royal Moldavian monastery, early to the painted-church program
sites.description: The monastery of 1530 that was among the first to receive the full external fresco program, a royal foundation, and burial place of Petru Rareș. UNESCO-listed among the painted churches of Moldavia.

sites.name: Princely Church of St. Nicholas
sites.address: Curtea de Argeș, Argeș County, Romania
sites.summary: The 14th-century Wallachian court church, with Romania's finest Byzantine-style frescoes
sites.description: The court church of the early Wallachian princes at Curtea de Argeș, built around the 1350s–60s and covered inside with an outstanding fresco cycle in the pure late-Byzantine manner. This may be the finest Byzantine-style painting in Romania.

sites.name: Basarabi-Murfatlar cave complex
sites.summary: A 10th-century chalk-cut cave-church complex of early Christian Dobruja
sites.description: A cluster of small churches, cells and galleries cut into a chalk hill in the tenth century and covered with early Slavic and Greek inscriptions and graffiti. This is a rare monument of the first Christian centuries of medieval Dobruja under Byzantine influence.

sites.name: Păcuiul lui Soare
sites.summary: A 10th-century Byzantine Danube fortress and naval base on an island
sites.description: The remains of a large tenth-century Byzantine fortress and naval base on a Danube island, built under the emperor John Tzimiskes as part of the reconquest of the lower Danube frontier. You must take a boat to visit.

sites.name: Capidava Fortress
sites.summary: A Roman-Byzantine Danube frontier fort, refortified under Justinian
sites.description: A Roman and early-Byzantine fort on the right bank of the Danube, part of the imperial frontier defenses, refortified in the sixth century and reoccupied in the tenth.

sites.name: Dinogetia Fortress
sites.summary: A lower-Danube Byzantine fort with a small 10th–11th-century church
sites.description: A late-Roman and Byzantine fort on the lower Danube, refortified under the early Byzantine emperors and again in the tenth to eleventh centuries, when a small church was built within the walls.

sites.name: Carsium Fortress
sites.summary: A Danube frontier fortress of Roman and Byzantine Scythia Minor
sites.description: A Roman and Byzantine fortress at Hârșova on the Danube, refortified in the sixth century and again in the middle Byzantine period as part of the frontier defenses of Scythia Minor.

sites.name: Ancient City of Histria
sites.summary: The oldest Greek city in Romania, with early-Byzantine basilicas by the sea
sites.description: The oldest Greek city on Romanian soil, on the Black Sea coast, which lived on as a fortified early-Byzantine town with several basilicas before decline in the seventh century. Extensively excavated.

sites.name: Tomis Archaeological Park
sites.summary: Ancient Constanța, a Byzantine metropolitan see with a great mosaic edifice
sites.description: The ancient port beneath modern Constanța, a metropolitan see of early-Byzantine Scythia Minor, whose remains include a great early-Christian basilica and a celebrated mosaic-floored commercial edifice by the harbor.

sites.name: Densuș Church
sites.summary: An ancient Transylvanian stone church of Roman spolia, with Byzantine-style fresco
sites.description: One of the oldest churches in Romania still in use, an idiosyncratic stone church at Densuș partly built of Roman spolia from nearby Ulpia Traiana, keeping fourteenth-century frescoes in the Byzantine tradition.

sites.name: Streisângeorgiu Church
sites.summary: A small Transylvanian church with some of the region's oldest Byzantine-style fresco
sites.description: A small Transylvanian church with a stone core of the late twelfth or early thirteenth century, keeping some of the oldest dated frescoes in the region, painted in the Byzantine manner for a local Romanian (Vlach) elite.

sites.name: Strei Church
sites.summary: A 14th-century Transylvanian church mixing Byzantine and Gothic painting
sites.description: A small stone church at Strei, built in the early fourteenth century, its frescoes blending Byzantine iconography with Western Gothic elements; a style typical of Orthodox Transylvania under Hungarian rule.

sites.name: Church of All Saints Sunday
sites.address: Râu de Mori, Hunedoara County, Romania
sites.summary: A Hațeg church with frescoes of the Byzantine-Orthodox Vlach nobility
sites.description: A medieval church in the Hațeg region tied to the Cândea (Kendeffy) family, keeping frescoes in the Byzantine-Orthodox tradition of the local Romanian nobility.

sites.name: St. Nicholas Church
sites.summary: A 1417 Transylvanian noble church with Byzantine-style founder portraits
sites.description: A church founded in 1417 at Ribița by local Romanian nobles and covered with frescoes in the Byzantine manner, including a rare portrayal of the founders.

sites.name: St. Catherine's Monastery
alternateNames: Sacred Monastery of the God-Trodden Mount Sinai
sites.summary: Justinian's Sinai fortress-monastery, still living, with the world's greatest early-icon collection
sites.description: One of the most important Byzantine sites anywhere, and never once conquered or abandoned. Justinian fortified the monastery around 548–565 around the older Chapel of the Burning Bush, and it has run as a Greek Orthodox house ever since. Its apse holds a superb Transfiguration mosaic of about 565, and its icon collection is the greatest on earth. The pre-Iconoclast encaustic panels survived precisely because remote Sinai lay beyond the reach of imperial Iconoclasm.

sites.name: Abu Mena
sites.address: Abu Mena, Borg El Arab, Alexandria Governorate, Egypt
sites.summary: The vast ruined pilgrimage city of St. Menas, its holy-oil flasks found across Europe
sites.description: The ruined pilgrimage city of Saint Menas, southwest of Alexandria and one of the great destinations of the late-antique Mediterranean. A basilica rose under Arcadius around 400 and Zeno added a vast transept basilica, creating a complex of churches, baths, and hostels; the little terracotta ampullae pilgrims carried home have turned up across Europe.

sites.name: Babylon Fortress
sites.summary: The banded Roman-Byzantine fortress under Old Cairo, held seven months against the Arab conquest
sites.description: The banded Roman fortress that anchors Old Cairo, the most substantial piece of imperial secular fabric in Egypt outside Alexandria. Built around 300 under Diocletian, its enclosure now holds the Coptic Museum and several churches, though those are largely post-conquest Coptic foundations.

sites.name: Kom el-Dikka
sites.summary: The excavated auditoria of Byzantine Alexandria, and the Mediterranean's only known ancient "university"
sites.description: A rare window onto late-antique Byzantine Alexandria, excavated in the heart of the modern city. Between the fourth and seventh centuries the district became a civic and academic quarter, and its standout is a complex of some twenty lecture halls and the mosaic-floored Villa of the Birds. The great Byzantine churches of Alexandria are gone; what survives here is the secular and intellectual fabric.

sites.name: Red Monastery
sites.summary: A Coptic triconch church holding Egypt's finest late-antique wall paintings
sites.description: A triconch sanctuary carpeted in densely layered fifth- and sixth-century wall paintings, whose recent cleaning has recovered their original brilliance. They may be ranked among the most important early Christian painting anywhere. A Coptic, non-Chalcedonian foundation, so its tie to Constantinople is stylistic rather than institutional. Still an active monastery.

sites.name: White Monastery
sites.summary: Shenoute's vast limestone monastery-basilica near Sohag, best paired with the Red Monastery
sites.description: This monastery's fortress-like limestone basilica was one of the largest churches in the country, serving a community that numbered in the thousands. Much of the interior is lost. A Coptic, non-Chalcedonian foundation, Byzantine-era in date but not imperial in allegiance.

sites.name: Philae
sites.summary: The Temple of Isis, closed by Justinian and converted to a church of St Stephen
sites.description: The island temple of Isis was the last functioning pagan sanctuary in the Roman world until, around 535–537, Justinian sent his general Narses to close it by force; the hypostyle hall was then turned into a church of St. Stephen, and the crosses, Greek inscriptions, and effaced reliefs cut by the new occupants are still legible over the pharaonic carving. The whole complex was moved to nearby Agilkia Island in the 1970s–80s to escape the Aswan dams, so its setting is modern.

sites.name: Qasr Libya
sites.address: Qasr Libya, Jabal al Akhdar, Libya
sites.summary: Justinian's Theodorias, whose church floor holds North Africa's finest Byzantine mosaics
sites.description: In 539 Justinian refounded the decayed town of Olbia and renamed it Theodorias for his wife Theodora. Its eastern church preserved a floor of some fifty mid-sixth-century mosaic panels with a celebrated image of the Pharos lighthouse of Alexandria. The pairing of the four rivers of Paradise with the Castalian Spring of Delphi shows a designer bracketing biblical and Greek wisdom. Among the finest Byzantine mosaics in North Africa.

sites.name: Ancient city of Apollonia
sites.address: Marsa Susa (Susa), Jabal al Akhdar, Libya
sites.summary: The Byzantine provincial capital of the Pentapolis, its churches and drowned harbor on the sea
sites.description: The port of Cyrene that outstripped its parent city: by the sixth century Apollonia, renamed Sozusa, was capital of the province of Libya Pentapolitana. It is among the richest Byzantine townscapes on the Cyrenaican coast, with three excavated churches, a sixth-century fortress, and a courtyard building long known as the “Palace of the Dux.” Part of the ancient harbor has sunk beneath the sea, so ruins lie visible in the shallows.

sites.name: Byzantine Church, Ras al-Hilal
sites.address: Ras al-Hilal, Jabal al Akhdar, Libya
sites.summary: A ruined sixth-century basilica on a Cyrenaican clifftop, east of Apollonia
sites.description: Atop the "Crescent Cape" stands the ruins of a sixth-century basilica traditionally linked to Justinian's building program in Cyrenaica. A conventional three-aisled late-antique church.

sites.name: Cyrene
sites.summary: The "Athens of Africa," a monumental Greek city with a modest Byzantine church layer
sites.description: The great Greek city of the Pentapolis is overwhelmingly classical but carries a real Byzantine layer. The standing Byzantine remains, a cathedral and lesser churches inserted into the older cityscape, are modest beside the Greek temples and necropolis.

sites.name: Ptolemais
sites.summary: A Pentapolis city where the philosopher-bishop Synesius served, over a Roman-Byzantine layer
sites.description: One of the five Pentapolis cities and, under Diocletian, capital of Libya Superior before the role passed to Apollonia. Principally a Greek and Roman site, but it stayed an inhabited, bishopric-bearing town through the Byzantine period, leaving a late-antique layer of churches, cisterns, and fortifications.

sites.name: Basilica of Justinian Sabratha
sites.summary: A Justinianic-era mosaic-floored basilica set into Roman Sabratha
sites.description: Sabratha is famous for its Roman theater, but its Byzantine chapter is genuine and datable. After Belisarius recovered Tripolitania from the Vandals in 533–534, the reconquered cities got new Nicene churches, and this basilica went up in the 530s using columns salvaged from earlier buildings. Its glory was its floor, with fine polychrome mosaic pavements, among the best from Byzantine North Africa, now largely lifted into the site museum.

sites.name: Byzantine Church at Leptis Magna
alternateNames: Church of the Theotokos, Leptis Magna
sites.summary: Justinian's churches inserted into Leptis Magna, attested by Procopius himself
sites.description: The grandest Roman city in Africa, with a modest but unusually well-documented Byzantine layer: Procopius records that after Belisarius took Leptis, Justinian dedicated multiple churches here. The principal church was installed inside the Severan Basilica while a smaller basilica was fitted into an old house on the Colonnaded Street, its columns reused from collapsed buildings.

sites.name: Göreme Open-Air Museum
sites.summary: A valley of rock-cut Byzantine churches, the core of monastic Cappadocia
sites.description: The heart of Byzantine Cappadocia: a dense cluster of rock-cut churches, chapels and refectories carved into the tufa of a monastic valley, most decorated between the tenth and twelfth centuries. Several keep vivid fresco cycles, and it is the single best introduction to the region's cave monasticism. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Tokalı Kilise
sites.summary: Cappadocia's largest rock church, with a superb blue-ground fresco cycle
sites.description: The largest rock-cut church in Cappadocia, just below the Göreme museum, its walls covered with an exceptional tenth-century cycle of the life of Christ set against a deep lapis-blue ground. It stands among the finest Byzantine painting in the region.

sites.name: Karanlık Kilise
sites.summary: Göreme's best-preserved church, its dim interior saving a brilliant fresco cycle
sites.description: The best-preserved of the Göreme churches, so called because little light reaches its interior, which is exactly why its late-eleventh-century frescoes keep such brilliant color. A near-complete New Testament cycle covers its domes and vaults.

sites.name: Ihlara Valley Churches
sites.summary: A river gorge lined with rock-cut churches, some of Cappadocia's earliest
sites.description: A deep volcanic gorge along the Melendiz river honeycombed with rock-cut churches, some among the earliest in Cappadocia. Their frescoes range from austere, cross-heavy iconoclast-era schemes to rich narrative cycles painted between the ninth and eleventh centuries. The Ağaçaltı and Kokar churches are the best known.

sites.name: Selime Monastery
sites.summary: Cappadocia's largest rock-cut monastery, a cathedral hollowed from a stone cone
sites.description: The largest rock-cut religious building in Cappadocia, a cathedral-scale monastery carved into a towering cone at the mouth of the Ihlara valley, with a basilical church, kitchens, stables and living quarters all hollowed from the rock in the tenth to eleventh century.

sites.name: Çavuşin Church
alternateNames: Church of St John the Baptist, Çavuşin
sites.summary: A cliff-top basilical church at Çavuşin, linked to the emperor Nikephoros Phokas
sites.description: An old basilical rock church on the cliff above the village of Çavuşin, dedicated to St. John the Baptist and among the largest and earliest in the region. A nearby church carries a famous painted procession commemorating the emperor Nikephoros Phokas, who passed through in 964–965.

sites.name: Derinkuyu Underground City
sites.summary: A vast multi-level underground refuge city, expanded by Byzantine Christians against raids
sites.description: The deepest of Cappadocia's underground cities, an eight-level warren of tunnels, halls, wells and a rock-cut churches that could shelter thousands. Cut into the soft tufa and much expanded in the Byzantine centuries as a refuge from Arab raids, it could be sealed from within by great rolling stone doors.

sites.name: Church of Mary
sites.summary: The church of the Council of Ephesus (431), where Mary was proclaimed Theotokos
sites.description: The long, much-rebuilt church along the north edge of Ephesus, fitted into an earlier Roman civic hall, traditionally the first church dedicated to the Virgin Mary and the setting of the Council of Ephesus in 431 that proclaimed her Theotokos. Also called the Double Church for its successive rebuildings.

sites.name: Cave of the Seven Sleepers
sites.summary: The Ephesian grotto and tomb-church of the legendary Seven Sleepers
sites.description: A hillside grotto and church-and-tomb complex on the slope of Mount Pion at Ephesus, venerated as the resting place of the Seven Sleepers, Christian youths who in the legend slept in a cave for two centuries. A pilgrimage cult grew here in the fifth century, leaving a warren of rock-cut tombs and a small church.

sites.name: Great Lavra
sites.summary: The first and senior monastery of Athos, founded in 963 by Athanasios the Athonite
sites.description: The oldest and senior of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos, founded in 963 by St. Athanasios the Athonite with the backing of the emperor Nikephoros Phokas. Its katholikon set the architectural model for the Holy Mountain, and it holds important relics, manuscripts and post-Byzantine frescoes by Theophanes the Cretan.

sites.name: Vatopedi Monastery
sites.summary: A great tenth-century Athonite monastery, rich in Byzantine mosaics and relics
sites.description: One of the greatest and wealthiest houses of Athos, founded in the late tenth century and ranking second in the hierarchy. It preserves outstanding Byzantine mosaics, a celebrated library of manuscripts, and revered relics including the girdle of the Virgin.

sites.name: Hilandar Monastery
sites.summary: The Serbian monastery of Athos, refounded by St. Sava in 1198
sites.description: The great Serbian monastery of the Holy Mountain, refounded in 1198 by St. Sava and his father Stefan Nemanja and long the spiritual and cultural heart of medieval Serbia. It keeps important frescoes, icons and one of the richest collections of medieval Slavic manuscripts and charters.

sites.name: Protaton
sites.summary: The mother church of Athos at Karyes, with Panselinos's great 14th-century frescoes
sites.description: The oldest church on Athos, in the capital Karyes, and the seat of the Holy Community that governs the mountain. Its walls carry the celebrated early-fourteenth-century frescoes attributed to Manuel Panselinos, the masterwork of late-Byzantine Macedonian school painting.

sites.name: Dionysiou Monastery
sites.summary: A cliff-top Athonite monastery of c.1375, endowed by the emperor of Trebizond
