sites.description: A dramatic monastery perched on a cliff above the southwest shore, founded around 1375 by St. Dionysios with the patronage of Alexios III, emperor of Trebizond, whose chrysobull survives here. It preserves fine late-Byzantine frescoes and a rich treasury.

sites.name: Boyana Church
sites.summary: A little Sofia church holding the extraordinary, lifelike frescoes of 1259
sites.description: A small church on the edge of Sofia, world-famous for the frescoes painted in 1259: 240 figures of startling, almost proto-Renaissance naturalism that mark a high point of late-Byzantine painting. The oldest eastern chapel goes back to the tenth or eleventh century. UNESCO-listed.

sites.name: Old Metropolitan Church
sites.summary: The early-Christian cathedral of Mesembria, a roofless basilica over the Black Sea town
sites.description: The roofless basilica at the heart of old Mesembria, the town's original cathedral, first built in the fifth or sixth century and rebuilt in the ninth. Its tall arcaded walls dominate the peninsula town that preserves more medieval churches than almost anywhere on the Black Sea.

sites.name: Church of Christ Pantocrator
sites.summary: A gaudily decorated 13th–14th-century church, showpiece of Nessebar's late-Byzantine style
sites.description: One of the best-preserved of Nessebar's medieval churches, built in the thirteenth or fourteenth century and famous for the exuberant exterior typical of the late-Byzantine Black Sea style, with its banded brick and stone, blind arcading, ceramic rosettes and a meander frieze.

sites.name: Church of St Stephen
sites.summary: Nessebar's "New Metropolis," an 11th-century basilica covered in later murals
sites.description: The "New Metropolis" of Nessebar, an eleventh-century three-aisled basilica that took over as the town cathedral, its interior almost entirely covered with later murals. More than a thousand figures painted from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries over a Byzantine core.

sites.name: Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs
sites.address: g.k. Asenov, ул. „Свети Климент Охридски“ 22, 5000 Veliko Tarnovo, Bulgaria
sites.summary: Ivan Asen II's 1230 victory church and royal mausoleum in the Bulgarian capital
sites.description: The royal church of the Second Bulgarian Empire, built by Tsar Ivan Asen II in 1230 to mark his victory at Klokotnitsa, below the Tsarevets citadel in the capital Tarnovo. It holds famous inscribed royal columns and served as a royal mausoleum.

sites.name: Church of St. Simeon Stylites
sites.summary: Zeno's colossal cruciform pilgrimage church around St Simeon's pillar, near Aleppo
sites.description: One of the greatest surviving buildings of the early Byzantine world: a vast cruciform pilgrimage complex of four basilicas radiating from the octagonal court that enclosed the pillar of St. Simeon Stylites, who spent decades atop a column here. Built around 476–491 under the emperor Zeno, it was the largest church on earth in its day. A ruin, and at risk in the Syrian war.

sites.name: Resafa
sites.summary: The desert pilgrimage city of St. Sergius, its Byzantine walls and basilicas in the steppe
sites.description: A great walled pilgrimage city in the Syrian steppe, renamed Sergiopolis for the martyr St. Sergius, whose relics drew crowds from across the Byzantine and Persian worlds. Its massive gypsum walls, cisterns and the ruins of its sixth-century basilicas rise dramatically from the desert. Remote and, in the war years, exposed to looting.

sites.name: The Dead Cities (Serjilla)
sites.summary: The best-preserved of Syria's "Dead Cities," a fossil of rural Byzantine life
sites.description: Serjilla is the best-preserved of the "Dead Cities," which are hundreds of remarkably intact late-antique villages scattered across the limestone massif of northern Syria, abandoned by the tenth century and never built over. Their churches, houses, baths and olive-presses give an unmatched picture of rural Byzantine life.

sites.name: Apamea
sites.summary: A great colonnaded city on the Orontes, a Byzantine metropolitan see, heavily looted in the war
sites.description: A vast Greco-Roman city on the Orontes, its two-kilometer colonnaded avenue among the longest in the ancient world, that remained an important Byzantine center and metropolitan see with cathedral and churches until the Persian and Arab conquests. Notoriously ravaged by industrial-scale looting during the Syrian war.

sites.name: Cathedral of Saints Sergius, Bacchus and Leontius
sites.summary: An early-6th-century domed church at Bosra, a forerunner of Justinian's architecture
sites.description: One of the earliest and most influential domed churches in the East, built in 512–513 in the black-basalt city of Bosra. With a broad circular plan set within a square, this church anticipated the great domed churches of Justinian's age. Now largely ruined, but a key monument in the development of Byzantine architecture.

sites.name: Great Meteoron
sites.summary: The largest Meteora monastery, founded atop its rock pinnacle around 1350
sites.description: The largest and oldest of the monasteries perched atop the sandstone pinnacles of Meteora, founded around the mid-fourteenth century by St. Athanasios the Meteorite. Its katholikon of the Transfiguration keeps fine post-Byzantine frescoes, and the monastery crowns the most spectacular monastic landscape in the Orthodox world.

sites.name: Varlaam Monastery
sites.summary: The second great Meteora monastery, on a pinnacle first settled in the 14th century
sites.description: The second-largest of the Meteora monasteries, on a neighboring pinnacle first settled by the hermit Varlaam in the fourteenth century and rebuilt in the sixteenth. Its church of All Saints holds a celebrated fresco cycle by Frangos Katelanos of 1548.

sites.name: Holy Trinity Monastery
alternateNames: Holy Monastery of the Holy Trinity
sites.summary: The most vertiginous Meteora monastery, perched on a sheer rock tower
sites.description: The most dramatically sited of the Meteora houses, reached by steps cut into a sheer rock tower above the Pineios gorge and founded in the later fifteenth century. Long the hardest to reach, requiring a rope net for supplies and, indeed, people.
